content: Imaging techniques used for the antenatal detection of morbidly adherent placenta include ultrasound and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). Ultrasound is typically the first-line imaging modality due to its widespread availability, cost-effectiveness, and non-invasive nature. Key ultrasound findings suggestive of morbidly adherent placenta include the presence of placental lacunae, loss of the hypoechoic retroplacental zone, thinning or disruption of the uterine serosa-bladder interface, and abnormal Doppler flow patterns such as turbulent or chaotic blood flow. MRI is often employed as a complementary imaging tool, particularly in cases where ultrasound findings are inconclusive or when there is a need for more detailed evaluation of placental invasion into adjacent structures. MRI findings indicative of morbidly adherent placenta include dark intraplacental bands on T2-weighted images, abnormal uterine bulging, and disruption of the normal myometrial-placental interface. Both imaging modalities play a critical role in the prenatal diagnosis and management planning for patients with suspected morbidly adherent placenta, as early detection is essential to optimize maternal and fetal outcomes.
